blocks.content: This chapter opens a new module dedicated entirely to page replacement algorithms, the specific policies an operating system uses to decide which resident page to evict when physical memory is full and a new page needs to be loaded in, directly continuing from the demand paging and page faults chapters in the memory management module.

FIFO, first in first out, is the simplest possible page replacement policy, and studying it carefully is genuinely worthwhile precisely because its simplicity leads to a famous, counterintuitive weakness, known as Belady Anomaly, that every other algorithm in this module is implicitly trying to avoid.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396019-312621019.png
1. The Core Idea: Evict Whoever Arrived First
blocks.text: 1. The Core Idea: Evict Whoever Arrived First

blocks.content: FIFO page replacement uses exactly one piece of information to decide which page to evict: how long that page has been resident in memory. Whichever page was loaded earliest, regardless of whether it has been used constantly since then or not touched again at all, is the one chosen for eviction when a new page needs room.

This is implemented conceptually as a simple queue of currently resident pages, ordered strictly by arrival time. Every time a new page is loaded, it joins the back of the queue. Every time a page needs to be evicted, the page at the front of the queue, the oldest one, is removed.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396020-1597321.png
blocks.alt: The Core Idea: Evict Whoever Arrived First

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: FIFO evicts whichever currently resident page has been in memory the longest, using only arrival order, with no regard at all for how recently or how often that page has actually been used.
2. A Worked Example

Consider the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with exactly 3 physical frames available. Tracing through it page by page shows exactly how FIFO behaves in practice, including which accesses are faults, needing to load a page not currently resident, and which are hits, the page already sitting in one of the 3 frames.

blocks.content: Notice page 1 gets evicted to make room for page 4, following strict arrival order, even though page 1 is referenced again immediately afterward, producing an avoidable fault that an algorithm paying attention to actual usage patterns might have avoided.
3. Belady Anomaly: More Memory, More Faults
blocks.text: 3. Belady Anomaly: More Memory, More Faults

blocks.content: Intuition strongly suggests that adding more physical frames to a system should never make page fault behavior worse, more room to keep pages resident should, if anything, only help. FIFO specifically breaks this intuition in a genuinely surprising way, a phenomenon named Belady Anomaly after the researcher who first identified it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396020-111558106.png
blocks.alt: Belady Anomaly: More Memory, More Faults

blocks.content: Running the exact same reference string above with 4 frames instead of 3 under FIFO specifically produces MORE total page faults, not fewer, 10 faults instead of 9. This is not a trick or an edge case invented for a textbook, it is a real, reproducible property of FIFO arising directly from its blind reliance on arrival order alone.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396426-412687578.png
blocks.alt: Belady Anomaly: More Memory, More Faults

blocks.title: Why this matters beyond FIFO itself
blocks.content: Belady Anomaly is specifically a property of FIFO, not a universal law of page replacement. Certain other algorithms, most notably LRU covered in the next chapter, are proven to never exhibit this anomaly at all, which is one of the concrete, measurable reasons LRU is generally preferred over FIFO in real systems.
4. Why FIFO Ignoring Usage Patterns Is a Real Weakness
blocks.text: 4. Why FIFO Ignoring Usage Patterns Is a Real Weakness

blocks.content: The deeper problem Belady Anomaly exposes is that FIFO decision making is entirely blind to how a page is actually being used. A page referenced constantly, over and over, gets evicted the moment it happens to be the oldest resident page, exactly as readily as a page that was loaded once and never touched again.

This stands in sharp contrast to the theoretical ideal covered in the next chapter, the optimal algorithm, which evicts specifically based on which resident page will not be needed again for the longest time in the future. FIFO ignoring this entirely is precisely why it tends to perform meaningfully worse in practice than algorithms that do pay attention to actual reference patterns.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396427-626089315.png
blocks.alt: Why FIFO Ignoring Usage Patterns Is a Real Weakness

5. A Practical Improvement: Second Chance

FIFO simplicity is genuinely appealing, and rather than abandoning it entirely, a natural refinement exists that keeps the same basic queue structure while fixing its most obvious blind spot, evicting a page purely by age with zero regard for whether it has actually been used recently.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409396427-877812047.png

The second chance algorithm, covered in full in the next chapter, adds exactly one piece of additional information, a single reference bit per page, checked before actually evicting the page at the front of the queue, giving a recently used page one more chance to stay resident rather than being evicted purely for being the oldest.

7. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

items: Assuming FIFO evicts the least recently used page, confusing it with LRU, covered in the next chapter, when FIFO only tracks arrival order, not usage recency at all.
Assuming adding more physical frames can never make page fault behavior worse under any algorithm, when FIFO specifically and demonstrably can suffer exactly this counterintuitive Belady Anomaly.

Underestimating FIFO as too trivial to be asked about directly, when tracing a FIFO example by hand and correctly identifying a Belady Anomaly scenario is a genuinely common, concrete interview exercise.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to trace FIFO by hand on a given reference string, and be ready to explain Belady Anomaly precisely: more physical frames producing more page faults, specifically under FIFO, because eviction decisions rest entirely on arrival order with no regard for actual usage.

FIFO sets the baseline for this module: simple, predictable, and easy to reason about, but genuinely blind to usage patterns. The next chapter covers LRU, an algorithm built specifically to fix that blind spot directly.
